title_en: DRC-Rwanda: Joint Monitoring Committee acknowledges obstacles to implementation of peace agreement.
excerpt_en: Meeting on 2 October 2025 in Washington in the presence of representatives from the DRC, Rwanda, the United States, Qatar, Togo and the African Union, the joint monitoring committee for the peace agreement signed on 27…
body_en:
Meeting on 2 October 2025 in Washington in the presence of representatives from the DRC, Rwanda, the United States, Qatar, Togo and the African Union, the joint monitoring committee for the peace agreement signed on 27 June acknowledged the persistence of obstacles to its implementation, notably the neutralisation of the FDLR (Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda) and the withdrawal of Rwandan forces. While welcoming the agreement on the exchange of prisoners reached in Doha and the upcoming resumption of talks with the AFC/M23 scheduled for 6 October, the committee insisted on the need for effective compliance with the agreement, access for the ICRC (International Committee of the Red Cross) to detainees and the abandonment of all hostile rhetoric.

It also called for restraint in the face of tensions in Uvira and Walikale, and announced a new meeting after the joint security coordination mechanism meeting scheduled for the end of October 2025.

title: DRC-Rwanda: Kinshasa blocks signing of regional economic agreement at the last minute
excerpt: The Democratic Republic of Congo refused to sign the regional economic integration framework (CIER) negotiated with Rwanda under US mediation at the last minute, even though both delegations were ready to initial the…
title_en: DRC-Rwanda: Kinshasa blocks signing of regional economic agreement at the last minute
excerpt_en: The Democratic Republic of Congo refused to sign the regional economic integration framework (CIER) negotiated with Rwanda under US mediation at the last minute, even though both delegations were ready to initial the…
body_en:
The Democratic Republic of Congo refused to sign the regional economic integration framework (CIER) negotiated with Rwanda under US mediation at the last minute, even though both delegations were ready to initial the text on Friday 3 October during discussions in Washington, after several days of negotiations. According to Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe, President Felix Tshisekedi instructed his delegation not to sign, citing fears of a negative reaction from Congolese public opinion.

The CIER, the economic component of the peace process launched on 27 June 2025 in Washington, aimed to strengthen cooperation in the mining, industrial, energy, agri-food, tourism and health sectors, while building on the security commitments discussed within the framework of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (MCCS). Kigali rejects the argument that Kinshasa made the signing conditional on the prior withdrawal of its troops from the east of the country, describing this justification as a "media pretext".

excerpt_en: Deputy Prime Minister of the Interior Shabani Lukoo Bihango summoned the provincial deputies of Kongo-Central, members of the bureau and petitioners to Kinshasa for urgent consultations as political tensions intensify.
body_en:
Deputy Prime Minister of the Interior Shabani Lukoo Bihango summoned the provincial deputies of Kongo-Central, members of the bureau and petitioners to Kinshasa for urgent consultations as political tensions intensify. The crisis erupted on 30 September with the filing of five petitions against the provincial assembly's bureau at the start of the parliamentary session, before taking a legal turn on 1 October when MP Mantezolo referred the matter to the Constitutional Court.

Between political manoeuvring and legal action, the Kongo-Central case has now taken on national significance.

title: Maniema: Kasongo civil society organises "dead city" days and peaceful march to denounce insecurity
excerpt: Since Wednesday 1 October 2025, civil society in Kasongo, in Maniema province, has been staging "dead city" days, with schools, markets and shops closed in protest against growing insecurity in the region.
title_en: Maniema: Kasongo civil society organises "dead city" days and peaceful march to denounce insecurity
excerpt_en: Since Wednesday 1 October 2025, civil society in Kasongo, in Maniema province, has been staging "dead city" days, with schools, markets and shops closed in protest against growing insecurity in the region.
body_en:
Since Wednesday 1 October 2025, civil society in Kasongo, in Maniema province, has been staging "dead city" days, with schools, markets and shops closed in protest against growing insecurity in the region. The main motive for this mobilisation is the resurgence of banditry and armed robbery, which affect local populations on a daily basis, disrupt trade and limit access to basic services.

On Friday 3 October 2025, a peaceful march brought together members of civil society around a memorandum submitted to the territorial authority. The demonstrators are demanding, in particular, the immediate departure of certain military, police and administrative officials deemed incapable of protecting the population, and are calling for concrete measures to restore security and confidence in local institutions.

title_en: DRC: Bintou Keita urges the Security Council to translate its commitments into concrete progress.
excerpt_en: Speaking before the UN Security Council on Tuesday 30 September 2025, the head of MONSCO, Bintou Keita, denounced the persistent gap between decisions taken on paper and the reality on the ground in the DRC, where…
body_en:
Speaking before the UN Security Council on Tuesday 30 September 2025, the head of MONSCO, Bintou Keita, denounced the persistent gap between decisions taken on paper and the reality on the ground in the DRC, where violence and massacres continue, with more than 1,000 civilians killed since June in Ituri and North Kivu. Presenting the Secretary-General's quarterly report, she warned of a drastic drop in humanitarian funding, with only 14.8% of the 2025 response plan covered, and called for a permanent ceasefire and a lasting peace agreement.

While welcoming the diplomatic efforts of Doha and Washington, she urged the international community to translate its commitments into tangible progress for the Congolese people.

According to Governor Jean-Paul Mbwebwa Kapo, the Head of State will inaugurate the official university of Mbuji-Mayi, inspect several infrastructure projects and meet with local authorities to discuss the revival of the Bakwanga Mining Company (MIBA), a declining pillar of the economy.

This presidential visit is raising high hopes among the population, who see it as an opportunity to revitalise employment and reinvigorate construction projects in this long-marginalised province.

title_en: National dialogue in the DRC: the roadmap drawn up by religious denominations marks a decisive step
excerpt_en: On 3 October 2025, the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Bintou Keita, welcomed before the Security Council the initiative of the country's main…
body_en:
On 3 October 2025, the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Bintou Keita, welcomed before the Security Council the initiative of the country's main religious denominations, which have drawn up a roadmap for a national and inclusive dialogue. This initiative, supported by President Félix Tshisekedi, aims to establish a climate of trust conducive to the 2028 general elections.

The roadmap consists of four stages: the "Month of Peace", dialogue between experts, political dialogue bringing together the opposition, the majority and civil society, and finally an international conference on peace and good living in the Great Lakes region. Ms Keita stressed that without this initiative, the 2028 elections could take place in a climate of mistrust and insecurity.

title: DRC: State of siege extended in North Kivu and Ituri, debates over possible extension
excerpt: On Thursday 2 October 2025 in Kinshasa, the National Assembly and the Senate adopted a further extension of the state of siege in the provinces of North Kivu and Ituri, despite dissenting voices questioning its effectiveness.
title_en: DRC: State of siege extended in North Kivu and Ituri, debates over possible extension
excerpt_en: On Thursday 2 October 2025 in Kinshasa, the National Assembly and the Senate adopted a further extension of the state of siege in the provinces of North Kivu and Ituri, despite dissenting voices questioning its effectiveness.
body_en:
On Thursday 2 October 2025 in Kinshasa, the National Assembly and the Senate adopted a further extension of the state of siege in the provinces of North Kivu and Ituri, despite dissenting voices questioning its effectiveness. MP Daida Moleka, elected representative of Lukunga, argued for its extension to South Kivu, citing the growing activism of armed groups and the M23 rebellion, but this proposal was rejected by several elected representatives, particularly from North Kivu, who questioned the results achieved.

The interim president of the National Assembly, Isaac Jean Claude Tshilumbayi, undertook to forward this suggestion to the government while calling on parliamentarians to strengthen their support for the armed forces in the face of the ongoing security crisis.

title_en: DRC: Digitisation of import-export operations comes into effect on 5 October
excerpt_en: From 5 October 2025, all applications and renewals for import-export numbers in the Democratic Republic of Congo will have to go exclusively through the Single Window for Foreign Trade (GUICE), the Ministry of Foreign…
body_en:
From 5 October 2025, all applications and renewals for import-export numbers in the Democratic Republic of Congo will have to go exclusively through the Single Window for Foreign Trade (GUICE), the Ministry of Foreign Trade has announced. This reform, which is part of the modernisation of public services, will enable economic operators to carry out all procedures related to import, export and transit online, without having to travel.

The aim is to reduce delays and costs, enhance transparency and traceability, and bring the DRC into line with World Trade Organisation standards. This digitalisation marks a key step in improving the competitiveness of Congolese foreign trade.

excerpt: On Friday 3 October, President Félix Tshisekedi praised the joint efforts of the Government and the Central Bank of Congo (BCC), which have led to a 9.1% appreciation of the Congolese franc against the dollar since 19 September.
title_en: Congolese franc: Tshisekedi calls for speculation to be curbed despite currency appreciation
excerpt_en: On Friday 3 October, President Félix Tshisekedi praised the joint efforts of the Government and the Central Bank of Congo (BCC), which have led to a 9.1% appreciation of the Congolese franc against the dollar since 19 September.
body_en:
On Friday 3 October, President Félix Tshisekedi praised the joint efforts of the Government and the Central Bank of Congo (BCC), which have led to a 9.1% appreciation of the Congolese franc against the dollar since 19 September. However, he urged the executive to maintain strict budgetary discipline and take vigorous measures against speculative practices that weaken the market, particularly due to the rate disparities observed in Kinshasa.

According to the minutes of the Council of Ministers presented by Patrick Muyaya, this monetary improvement is the result of bank reserves, tax levies and targeted interventions by the BCC. Tshisekedi insisted on the need for a more innovative and coherent approach to sustainably strengthen the credibility and stability of the Congolese franc.

title_en: Kongo-Central: Judith Suminwa launches modernisation works on the Kwilu-Ngongo-Kimpangu road
excerpt_en: At the end of her tour of Kongo-Central, Prime Minister Judith Suminwa launched construction work on the Kwilu-Ngongo-Kimpangu toll road on Wednesday 1 October 2025, a project entrusted to the China Road and Bridge…
body_en:
At the end of her tour of Kongo-Central, Prime Minister Judith Suminwa launched construction work on the Kwilu-Ngongo-Kimpangu toll road on Wednesday 1 October 2025, a project entrusted to the China Road and Bridge Corporation and TECNOVIA consortium. With an estimated cost of USD 160.38 million, 20% of which is financed by the government and 80% by a bank loan, this project involves the modernisation of 96 km of dirt track into a two-lane asphalt road, the construction of a modern dry port in Kimpangu and the rehabilitation of urban roads.

Considered a strategic corridor linking National Road No. 1 to the Angolan border, this infrastructure is to be completed in 24 months and promises to boost the local economy, improve mobility and generate employment opportunities, a prospect welcomed with enthusiasm by users.

body_en:
Since 1 October 2025, twelve schools in the Waloa Yungu group in Masisi territory (North Kivu) have remained closed due to clashes between rebels from the AFC-M23 group, the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) and their Wazalendo allies. Among these establishments, seven primary and five secondary schools located in the localities of Bibatama and Mitwa, close to the borders of the Luberike group, are affected. The escalation of violence has caused parents, pupils and teachers to flee, with some taking refuge in the bush, leading to a mass displacement of the population and the suspension of school activities. The provincial education authorities are calling for security measures to be strengthened to enable the gradual return of the population and the reopening of schools, fearing that the school year will be lost if peace is not quickly restored.

title: DRC: Joseph Kabila sentenced to death by military high court for treason and war crimes
excerpt: On Tuesday, 30 September 2025, the military high court in Kinshasa sentenced former Congolese President Joseph Kabila to death, finding him guilty of treason, participation in an insurrectionary movement and war crimes.
title_en: DRC: Joseph Kabila sentenced to death by military high court for treason and war crimes
excerpt_en: On Tuesday, 30 September 2025, the military high court in Kinshasa sentenced former Congolese President Joseph Kabila to death, finding him guilty of treason, participation in an insurrectionary movement and war crimes.
body_en:
On Tuesday, 30 September 2025, the military high court in Kinshasa sentenced former Congolese President Joseph Kabila to death, finding him guilty of treason, participation in an insurrectionary movement and war crimes. Absent from the hearing, the senator for life was also ordered to pay $33 billion in damages, including $29 billion to the Congolese state and $2 billion to each of the provinces of North Kivu.

According to the court, Kabila leads the AFC/M23 rebel coalition and, together with Corneille Nangaa and Rwanda, is orchestrating a plan to overthrow the country's institutions by force. While dismissing the seizure of his assets and the question of his nationality, the verdict marks a major judicial and political turning point, causing a national uproar.

However, the Common Front for Congo (FCC), his political family, denounced the verdict as an "illegal conviction" and saw it as an exploitation of the justice system to undermine his moral authority. For this platform, it is a frontal attack on the rule of law and a dangerous democratic setback that plunges the DRC into a zone of political and institutional uncertainty.

On Friday, 3 October 2025, an armed group, believed to be affiliated with the ADF, was repelled about 9 kilometres from the centre of Bafwasende, in Tshopo province. The Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and local Wazalendo militiamen joined forces to counter this advance, after local youth had initially hindered the attackers' progress.

The clashes were reported near Buyuli, in the Bangbabi region, on the border of the Opienge territory. The situation caused widespread panic among the population, leading to mass displacement to Nia-Nia and Kisangani.

According to witnesses, heavy and light weapons fire could be heard as far away as central Bafwasende. Local authorities and civil society remain vigilant in the face of the persistent threat posed by the ADF in the region.

Since the end of September 2025, around 4,000 civilians, including nearly 1,950 women and 700 children, have taken refuge around the MONUSCO base in Gina, in the territory of Djugu, Ituri, fleeing intensified clashes between the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), CODECO militiamen and the Convention for Popular Revolution (CRP). Faced with gunfire in the town of Tcha-Toba, MONUSCO reinforced its patrols with armoured vehicles to secure access and protect the population, evacuating three wounded people to Bunia for specialised care.

The rapid intervention of the peacekeepers made it possible to limit human losses and secure civilians in an area regularly exposed to violence.

On 2 October 2025, the population of the Beni territory in North Kivu commemorated 11 years since the start of the massacres perpetrated by ADF rebels, which since 2014 have resulted in the deaths of at least 10,000 civilians and the displacement of entire villages. In Oicha, scientists, civil society actors and security officials organised a public forum to analyse the causes of the persistent insecurity and issued an urgent appeal to the government to strengthen its strategy for protecting the population.

Participants also recommended support measures, including tax exemptions for affected communities, to alleviate the suffering of a population traumatised by more than a decade of violence.

title_en: Luhihi: closure of mining site by M23 leads to surge in crime
excerpt_en: Since the closure of the Luhihi artisanal mining site by AFC/M23 rebels on 30 August 2025, the security situation has deteriorated significantly in this area located in the territory of Kabare and part of the city of…
body_en:
Since the closure of the Luhihi artisanal mining site by AFC/M23 rebels on 30 August 2025, the security situation has deteriorated significantly in this area located in the territory of Kabare and part of the city of Bukavu, in South Kivu. The ban on access to the site has led to a mass exodus of artisanal miners from North Kivu, South Kivu and neighbouring countries.

Since then, the area has been plagued by a resurgence of burglaries, armed assaults, thefts and murders, particularly in nearby neighbourhoods such as Mulambula, Cikonyi in Bagira, and Irambo in the commune of Ibanda, according to civil society. This citizen group attributes these acts to young people who have become idle since the site was closed.

Security agents deployed by M23 leaders have arrested at least four people suspected of committing these acts, but the situation remains difficult to contain, according to witnesses. A new armed incursion in Ishungu has left one person dead and several injured.

Mapenzi Manyebwa, a civil society activist, condemns this situation and calls for urgent action to restore security and end the spiral of violence.

body_en:
The Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC), supported by the Wazalendo militias, launched a counter-offensive on Tuesday 29 September 2025 to regain control of Nzibira, a strategic town in the Walungu territory recently occupied by AFC-M23 rebels. Fighting is concentrated around the Mulunga, Chirwa, Nyamarhege, Mulamba and Kaniola mountains, where the army is also using targeted drone strikes.

excerpt_en: A United Nations report published on 2 October 2025 reveals that the Rwandan-backed M23 armed group is responsible for serious human rights violations in North and South Kivu provinces.
body_en:
A United Nations report published on 2 October 2025 reveals that the Rwandan-backed M23 armed group is responsible for serious human rights violations in North and South Kivu provinces. Over the past three months, nearly 540 civilians have been summarily executed, including 325 in Rutshuru territory during anti-FDLR operations, including 52 women and 24 children in the Bwisha chiefdom.

At the same time, more than 1,450 people have been forcibly recruited into the M23 ranks and sent to training camps. Despite the ceasefire agreed under the Doha peace process, the rebels are continuing their offensives in Walikkale and Masisi, causing tensions to escalate.

In response, the Congolese air force has intensified its strikes against M23 positions, particularly in Buleusa, while the international community is calling for the protection of civilians and respect for humanitarian law.

title: Maniema: MSF announces early closure of its project in Salamabila due to lack of funding
excerpt: On 3 October 2025, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) announced the early closure, scheduled for the end of October, of its project to care for victims of sexual violence in Salamabila, Maniema, which was initially planned…
title_en: Maniema: MSF announces early closure of its project in Salamabila due to lack of funding
excerpt_en: On 3 October 2025, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) announced the early closure, scheduled for the end of October, of its project to care for victims of sexual violence in Salamabila, Maniema, which was initially planned…
body_en:
On 3 October 2025, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) announced the early closure, scheduled for the end of October, of its project to care for victims of sexual violence in Salamabila, Maniema, which was initially planned to run until 2026. After seven years of activity and more than 16,000 survivors treated since 2019, the NGO justifies this decision by the drastic drop in humanitarian funding, with only 15% of the response plan covered, and by the need to redirect its resources to other critical areas, particularly South Kivu. However, MSF stresses that it has achieved its objectives by developing a replicable community model, while maintaining a minimum response to health emergencies in the province, and calls on the authorities and donors to ensure the continuity of the achievements in order to avoid a breakdown in the protection of vulnerable populations.

Overall comment: This report highlights tensions in the DRC: diplomatic deadlock with Rwanda, internal political crises, persistent violence in the east, and social fragility exacerbated by poverty and epidemics. Despite some economic progress, such as the digitisation of foreign trade and the stabilisation of the Congolese franc, the benefits for the population remain limited.

In short, the country needs inclusive political dialogue, strengthened regional diplomacy, a reformed and better-equipped army, and urgent social measures to restore peace and national confidence.

title: DRC-Rwanda: Tshisekedi calls for dialogue while Kigali denounces "political theatre"
excerpt: On 9 October 2025, speaking at the Global Gateway Forum in Brussels, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi made a solemn appeal to his Rwandan counterpart Paul Kagame to turn the page on tensions in the Great Lakes region.
title_en: DRC-Rwanda: Tshisekedi calls for dialogue while Kigali denounces "political theatre"
excerpt_en: On 9 October 2025, speaking at the Global Gateway Forum in Brussels, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi made a solemn appeal to his Rwandan counterpart Paul Kagame to turn the page on tensions in the Great Lakes region.
body_en:
On 9 October 2025, speaking at the Global Gateway Forum in Brussels, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi made a solemn appeal to his Rwandan counterpart Paul Kagame to turn the page on tensions in the Great Lakes region. He called on Kigali to order an end to M23 hostilities and temporarily suspended his call for sanctions, stating that the DRC "wants real peace, the kind that leads to stability and development." In response, Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe described the initiative as "political theatre", accusing Tshisekedi of hijacking a cooperation forum and turning it into a platform for attacks, violating the peace agreements signed in Washington and supporting militias hostile to the Banyamulenge. According to Kigali, the Congolese president is seeking to influence domestic public opinion, whereas the issue of the DRC should be addressed in other regional negotiating forums.

However, President Félix Tshisekedi's olive branch to his Rwandan counterpart Paul Kagame has provoked an outcry among the Congolese opposition, which sees it as an inconsistent and short-sighted move. Claudel André Lubaya, national deputy and president of the UDA-Originel, criticised the head of state's "diplomatic versatility", while Olivier Kamitatu, former president of the National Assembly and spokesperson for Moïse Katumbi, described his comments as "empty words" disconnected from the realities of the country. For his part, Prince Epenge, spokesperson for the Lamuka coalition, believes that Tshisekedi should first seek "peace among the brave" with the Congolese themselves before reaching out to Kigali.

title_en: Kongo Central: Papy Mantezolo resigns as president of the Provincial Assembly under pressure from a motion
excerpt_en: The president of the Provincial Assembly of Kongo-Central, Papy Mantezolo, resigned on 6 October 2025, followed by his vice-president Joseph Nsalambi Ngabakita and rapporteur Victor Nsuami, after a motion of no…
body_en:
The president of the Provincial Assembly of Kongo-Central, Papy Mantezolo, resigned on 6 October 2025, followed by his vice-president Joseph Nsalambi Ngabakita and rapporteur Victor Nsuami, after a motion of no confidence signed by the majority of deputies accusing them of mismanagement and embezzlement of public funds. The plenary session scheduled to examine the motion was marred by violence that left several elected officials and journalists injured.

Mantezolo, denouncing a failure to follow procedures, said he was stepping down to preserve peace and cohesion within the institution. The session, relocated to Matadi Town Hall, ended with the installation of a bureau d'âge (provisional bureau) headed by Jean N'landu Nsongo, responsible for overseeing the rest of the parliamentary process.

body_en:
Following the violent incidents that took place on 6 October 2025 at the Provincial Assembly of Kongo-Central, where several MPs and journalists were injured, the Ministry of the Interior, through its adviser Jean-Marc Nzeyidio Lukombo, called on 7 October for peaceful coexistence and respect for the democratic process in provincial assemblies. He strongly condemned these acts, which he deemed unacceptable, pointing out that the installation of the bureau d'âge is a legal procedure that must take place in a calm atmosphere. This statement comes amid a tense political climate marked by the resignation of the president of the provincial assembly, Papy Mantezolo, and the relocation of the plenary session to the Matadi town hall to ensure that work can continue in a peaceful manner.

DRC: Kinshasa makes any economic agreement with Rwanda conditional on the withdrawal of its troops

On 8 October 2025, the Congolese government reaffirmed that no economic agreement will be signed with Rwanda as long as Rwandan troops remain deployed in eastern DRC alongside M23 rebels. According to spokesperson Patrick Muyaya, this position explains Kinshasa's refusal to sign the Regional Economic Integration Framework (CIER) proposed under US mediation in Washington. The government believes that lasting peace must precede any economic or diplomatic cooperation, denouncing in particular the massacres of civilians in Rutshuru as proof of continuing instability. According to Kinshasa, this decision is part of a diplomatic approach based on sovereignty and national security.

body_en:
A motion to remove Germaine Tshinyama, Vice-President of the Kinshasa Provincial Assembly, from office was tabled on 9 October 2025. This motion, initiated by MP Steve Mulumba, calls for a plenary session to be convened to examine the proposal in accordance with the rules of procedure of the Kinshasa Provincial Assembly.

More than 15 signatures have already been collected in support of this initiative. Germaine Tshinyama, who has been acting as interim president since Lévi Mbuta's temporary withdrawal for health reasons, could thus see her term cut short, marking a significant turning point in the provincial governance of the Congolese capital.

excerpt_en: Currently, more than 45,000 Congolese nationals living in Rwanda are sounding the alarm over the lack of consular services since Congolese diplomats were recalled to Kinshasa.
body_en:
Currently, more than 45,000 Congolese nationals living in Rwanda are sounding the alarm over the lack of consular services since Congolese diplomats were recalled to Kinshasa. Unable to renew their passports or obtain travel documents, many of them find themselves in an irregular situation, threatened with losing their jobs, their studies or access to healthcare.

Without valid documents, they can no longer carry out banking transactions or essential administrative procedures. The Congolese community is calling on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to urgently appoint a local agent in charge of day-to-day affairs to restore the necessary administrative and humanitarian assistance, while Kinshasa remains silent on this crisis.

title_en: DRC: André Wameso announces sustained appreciation of the Congolese franc
excerpt_en: On 9 October 2025, the Governor of the Central Bank of Congo (BCC), André Wameso, stated that, according to all market indicators, the Congolese franc will continue to appreciate.
body_en:
On 9 October 2025, the Governor of the Central Bank of Congo (BCC), André Wameso, stated that, according to all market indicators, the Congolese franc will continue to appreciate. This statement comes after a significant reduction in the BCC's key interest rate, from 25% to 17.5%, aimed at strengthening monetary stability and encouraging investment.

Wameso highlighted the BCC's efforts to restore confidence in the national currency, despite the challenges associated with downward price rigidity in the market. He also pointed out that the fall in the prices of imported goods, which are denominated in dollars, should follow this trend, although this process may take time.

This policy is part of the government's action programme to improve the purchasing power of the Congolese population.

According to the Secretary General for Foreign Trade, Jules Muilu Mbo, this system allows economic operators to centralise all their procedures online, reducing travel, delays and costs, while increasing the transparency and traceability of public revenues.

Training courses will soon be organised to support administrative staff and economic operators in all provinces.

title_en: DRC: teachers demand better socio-professional conditions

body_en:
On International Teachers' Day, 5 October, the Synergie des syndicats des enseignants de la RDC (Synergy of Teachers' Unions of the DRC) called on the government to urgently improve teachers' social and salary conditions. Meeting in Kinshasa, the unions denounced the precariousness of salaries, the lack of support for unpaid teachers, inadequate pensions and the absence of continuing training, stressing that these shortcomings hinder the quality of education.

They also warned of the negative effects of poorly supervised free education in primary schools, which increases the workload without compensation. The government, through the Minister of State for Education, Raïssa Malu, had nevertheless reaffirmed its commitment to improving these conditions despite budgetary and security constraints.

title_en: North Kivu: humanitarian aid truck set on fire by youths in Oicha
excerpt_en: A truck carrying humanitarian aid for displaced persons in Eringeti and Mayimoya was set on fire on the night of 7 to 8 October in Oicha, the capital of Beni territory in North Kivu.
body_en:
A truck carrying humanitarian aid for displaced persons in Eringeti and Mayimoya was set on fire on the night of 7 to 8 October in Oicha, the capital of Beni territory in North Kivu. According to witnesses, a group of youths intercepted two lorries on National Road 4, mistakenly suspecting that they were supplying armed groups, before setting fire to one of them.

The incident, which occurred near the mosque in the Masosi neighbourhood, destroyed the entire cargo. Local authorities, including Mayor Eugénie Kavira Mwenge, condemned the act and announced the opening of an investigation, while civil society called on young people to avoid all forms of violence or vigilante justice.

body_en:
The section of the Bukavu-Goma road near the village of Tchofi, in the Kalehe territory (South Kivu), remains severely damaged due to heavy rains and landslides, making it difficult, if not impossible, for vehicles and motorcycles to travel on it. The Kalinga River has burst its banks and threatens to cut off the road, isolating the towns of Tchofi and Nyabibwe and disrupting socio-economic activities.

Residents are calling on the authorities to intervene quickly with heavy machinery, as the promises of rehabilitation made in June 2025 by AFC-M23 rebel leaders have not yet been fulfilled. This situation is compounded by recurrent armed conflict, exacerbating access difficulties and the precarious situation of local populations.

On World Mental Health Day on 10 October 2025, the South Kivu Provincial Health Division revealed that 118,379 cases of mental disorders had been recorded in the first half of the year. Among them, 10,888 cases of post-traumatic stress disorder, 6,171 cases of depression, 2,437 cases of drug addiction and 93 suicides were recorded.

This report highlights the impact of armed conflict, poverty and violence on the psychological health of populations, particularly women and children. Health authorities are calling for the urgent integration of mental health into primary health care in order to strengthen prevention, treatment and community awareness.

title: DRC: CENCO says it is "horrified" by Joseph Kabila's death sentence
excerpt: On 6 October 2025, the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) expressed its indignation at the High Military Court's verdict sentencing former President Joseph Kabila to death.
title_en: DRC: CENCO says it is "horrified" by Joseph Kabila's death sentence
excerpt_en: On 6 October 2025, the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) expressed its indignation at the High Military Court's verdict sentencing former President Joseph Kabila to death.
body_en:
On 6 October 2025, the National Episcopal Conference of Congo (CENCO) expressed its indignation at the High Military Court's verdict sentencing former President Joseph Kabila to death. In a statement signed by its secretary general, Mgr Donatien Nshole, CENCO reaffirmed its firm opposition to capital punishment, considering it a violation of the fundamental right to life enshrined in the Constitution and divine law.

The Catholic bishops denounced the decision as hasty and incompatible with the spirit of the Gospel, recalling that they had already called for the abolition of the death penalty after the moratorium was lifted in 2024. For them, this sentence marks a serious setback in the defence of human dignity in the DRC.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of the Interior Jacquemain Shabani, warned of the growing influx of refugees into the Democratic Republic of Congo, estimated at more than 88,000 people from South Sudan and the Central African Republic, during the 76th session of the UNHCR Executive Committee held from 6 to 10 October 2025 in Geneva. According to him, this return will only be possible after an effective ceasefire, the restoration of state authority and the verification of the nationality of those wishing to return.

body_en:
Between 28 September and 8 October 2025, violent fighting broke out between M23 rebels and the Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) in the chiefdoms of Bwito and Bahunde in North Kivu, leaving at least 4 dead, 13 missing and 8 women raped, according to civil society. These clashes resulted in the burning of several homes, including the Nyabiteja primary school, as well as the looting of the Muliki health centre and the theft of around 20 cattle.

The communities of Bukombo, Tongo, Bambo, Mutanda, Kihondo and Ufamandu 1er were among the worst affected. As people flee to Bambo, Kabizo, Butare and Ngungu, civil society organisations are denouncing serious human rights violations and urging the authorities to strengthen the protection of civilians in this region, which is plagued by persistent insecurity.

excerpt: At least eight people were killed on Wednesday, 7 October 2025, in an ambush by CODECO militiamen in the village of Kalanda, about 30 kilometres north of Bunia, in the territory of Djugu (Ituri).
title_en: Ituri: Eight civilians killed in an ambush by CODECO militiamen in Djugu
excerpt_en: At least eight people were killed on Wednesday, 7 October 2025, in an ambush by CODECO militiamen in the village of Kalanda, about 30 kilometres north of Bunia, in the territory of Djugu (Ituri).

At least eight people were killed on Wednesday, 7 October 2025, in an ambush by CODECO militiamen in the village of Kalanda, about 30 kilometres north of Bunia, in the territory of Djugu (Ituri). According to witnesses, the victims-farmers from the localities of Chilu, Susudd'ale, and Gobba-were captured, interrogated, and then executed before being mutilated, causing widespread outrage among the population.

While some sources mention a clash between armed groups, civil society rejects this theory and denounces the passivity of the FARDC stationed in Luvangire, accusing them of failing to react in time. It is calling for an urgent investigation to identify the perpetrators and for the bodies to be returned to the bereaved families, while the Congolese army has not yet made any official statement.

title_en: North Kivu and Ituri: UPDF proposes the establishment of local defence structures to counter ADF attacks
excerpt_en: In response to the intensification of massacres perpetrated by the ADF in North Kivu and Ituri, Ugandan Major General Stéphane Mugerwa, a partner of the FARDC in the joint "Shujaa" operations, suggested on 7 October…
body_en:
In response to the intensification of massacres perpetrated by the ADF in North Kivu and Ituri, Ugandan Major General Stéphane Mugerwa, a partner of the FARDC in the joint "Shujaa" operations, suggested on 7 October 2025 the creation of local defence structures to protect the population during jihadist incursions. According to him, these local defenders could secure towns and villages while the FARDC and UPDF operate in the hinterland. This idea, already raised by Congolese authorities since 2021, has been revived in a context where ADF attacks have killed dozens of people in recent months, particularly in Komanda, Beni and Ntoyo, and where the enemy continues to bypass military positions to strike unprotected villages. Local actors and legal experts stress that the implementation of this initiative would require a strict legal framework to arm certain civilians in self-defence, in a context where military operations alone have not been sufficient to stem the threat.

The period from late September to mid-October 2025 marked a tense turning point for the Democratic Republic of Congo, where diplomacy, security, and governance remain closely intertwined. Despite renewed peace efforts under the Doha and Washington agreements, strained relations between Kinshasa and Kigali and the continued M23 offensives in North and South Kivu highlighted the fragility of regional stability. Domestically, political turbulence-from crises within provincial assemblies to corruption investigations-reflected persistent institutional weaknesses. Economically, the government sought to demonstrate progress through currency stabilization, the digitalization of trade, and major infrastructure and energy agreements. However, these advances contrast sharply with social hardship, persistent violence, and humanitarian crises. Overall, the DRC finds itself at a crossroads: while international partners advocate reform and peace, the gap between commitments and reality on the ground continues to define the Congolese landscape.

title: President Tiani Visits Mali to Strengthen Sahel Security Cooperation
excerpt: BAMAKO, Mali - Niger’s President, General Abdourahamane Tiani, conducted a friendship and working visit to Bamako on September 30, marking his second official trip to Mali since assuming power in July 2023.
title_en: President Tiani Visits Mali to Strengthen Sahel Security Cooperation
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - Niger’s President, General Abdourahamane Tiani, conducted a friendship and working visit to Bamako on September 30, marking his second official trip to Mali since assuming power in July 2023.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - Niger’s President, General Abdourahamane Tiani, conducted a friendship and working visit to Bamako on September 30, marking his second official trip to Mali since assuming power in July 2023.

The visit underscored the growing military and political coordination within the Alliance of Sahel States (AES). Following a one-on-one meeting with Malian President Assimi Goïta, the two leaders held an extended working session attended by senior officials, including the defense ministers of both nations.

Discussions centered on the fight against terrorism and the accelerating security deterioration across the Sahel. The two presidents agreed to fast-track the operationalization of the AES joint military force, a unified command structure designed to enhance coordinated counterterrorism operations.

President Tiani emphasized that the creation of joint battalions composed of Nigerien, Malian, and Burkinabè soldiers would represent a decisive step toward collective security and sovereignty in the region. The move reflects the alliance’s broader vision of self-reliant defense and regional stability free from external dependency.

title: High Court Dismisses Case Challenging Dissolution of Political Parties
excerpt: BAMAKO, Mali - The High Court of Bamako’s 6th district this week rejected a complaint filed by political parties challenging the transitional government’s decision to dissolve them.
title_en: High Court Dismisses Case Challenging Dissolution of Political Parties
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - The High Court of Bamako’s 6th district this week rejected a complaint filed by political parties challenging the transitional government’s decision to dissolve them.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - The High Court of Bamako’s 6th district this week rejected a complaint filed by political parties challenging the transitional government’s decision to dissolve them. The court ruled the petition unfounded, effectively upholding the government’s actions.

The political parties have indicated they may appeal the decision. Other proceedings related to the case are ongoing in both lower courts and the Constitutional Court.

Mountaga Tall, one of the parties’ lawyers, explained that the main objective was to have the repeal of the Political Parties Charter - the legal basis for the dissolution decree - reviewed by the Constitutional Court. The High Court route was pursued with the support of members of the National Transitional Council (CNT), but this approach proved difficult under current political conditions. Legal experts note that, alternatively, parties could raise an exception of unconstitutionality before a court, which would then refer the matter to the Constitutional Court via the Supreme Court.

title_en: Mali Harmonizes Passport Prices with AES Confederation
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - The Malian Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree on Wednesday standardizing passport prices in line with the Confederation of Sahel States (AES) travel document framework.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - The Malian Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree on Wednesday standardizing passport prices in line with the Confederation of Sahel States (AES) travel document framework. The move aims to facilitate free movement of people, goods, and services amid ongoing regional security challenges.

The AES e-passport, introduced on April 18, 2025, meets International Civil Aviation Organization standards and protects personal data. Under the new decree, the standard passport service is set at 45,000 CFA francs, while the premium service costs 90,000 CFA francs - reductions of 10,000 and 20,000 CFA francs respectively from previous rates.

Following Mali’s withdrawal from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger launched the common passport earlier this year, with prices now harmonized across the three countries.

excerpt_en: MALI - Economic activity across Mali has slowed sharply following a terrorist-imposed blockade on hydrocarbon imports that began in mid-September.
body_en:
MALI - Economic activity across Mali has slowed sharply following a terrorist-imposed blockade on hydrocarbon imports that began in mid-September. The disruption has triggered severe fuel shortages in regional capitals including Koutiala, Nioro du Sahel, and Ségou, as well as in hundreds of rural sub-prefectures.

Vehicles of all types have been immobilized, and prolonged power outages have plunged many towns into darkness - some for an entire week. According to authorities, more than 100 tanker trucks have been burned by armed groups since the blockade began.

Although the army is providing escorts for convoys, attacks persist, discouraging transporters from resuming deliveries. The capital and border cities remain relatively stable, but national energy output has fallen drastically - from 18 hours of power per day to barely six.

title_en: Fuel Shortages Cause Widespread Disruption Across Mali
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - Mali is grappling with a severe fuel crisis, as long queues form daily at gas stations, with motorists often waiting three to four hours for a few liters of gasoline.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - Mali is grappling with a severe fuel crisis, as long queues form daily at gas stations, with motorists often waiting three to four hours for a few liters of gasoline. Since October 7, only about 10% of gas stations have been operational, with regions like Mopti, Koutiala, and Ségou experiencing outages for over ten days.

The shortages are attributed to a blockade imposed by terrorists, forcing fuel convoys to travel under army escort.

On October 8, 300 tanker trucks arrived in Bamako under military protection, temporarily easing supply for the capital. However, by October 11, refueling challenges resurfaced, and many regions remain without access to fuel.

The crisis has caused urban transport costs to surge, with taxi and motorcycle fares doubling, and bicycles becoming the primary mode of transportation in some areas. In response, the Customs Directorate General has announced 24-hour operations at the petroleum products office to facilitate timely declaration processing and support importers.

body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - The ongoing fuel crisis in Mali is severely disrupting electricity supply, with more than 80% of the country’s energy generated from thermal sources. Mopti, the nation’s fifth-largest city, has been completely without electricity for the past ten days, causing hospitals and essential services to operate at a reduced capacity.

In the capital, Bamako, power availability has dropped to just six hours per day, affecting public and private sector operations. Prior to the fuel blockade imposed by terrorist groups, cities already faced energy challenges, but electricity supply was significantly higher - Bamako previously had 19 hours of daily power.

Experts warn that unless a resolution is reached with the armed groups, Mali could face a nationwide standstill within two weeks, risking public unrest and increased terrorist proximity to urban centers.

title_en: Mali Awards Mining Rights to U.S. Firm Flagship, Signaling Strategic Sector Revival
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - On October 8, the Malian government took a decisive step to revitalize its gold mining sector, signing an agreement with U.S.-based company Flagship to resume production at the Morila gold mine, one of…
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - On October 8, the Malian government took a decisive step to revitalize its gold mining sector, signing an agreement with U.S.-based company Flagship to resume production at the Morila gold mine, one of the country’s most prominent mineral assets. The deal was formalized by the Société de Recherche et d’Exploitation des Ressources Minérales du Mali (SOREM), which owns full capital of the mine in southern Mali.

Minister of Mines, Prof. Amadou Keita, highlighted the significance of the agreement as part of SOREM’s operationalization, a state-owned entity established under the directive of President Assimi Goïta to ensure that Mali’s mineral wealth directly contributes to national development. “The reforms undertaken aim to bring the mining sector back under state control within a framework of win-win partnerships with investors,” said Keita, urging SOREM to execute its mandate with diligence.

Economy and Finance Minister Alousséni Sanou echoed the optimism, noting that the Morila mine, which holds estimated reserves of 2.5 million ounces of gold, has the potential to catalyze economic growth following a nearly two-year shutdown.

Analysts view the agreement as part of Mali’s broader geopolitical and economic strategy. In recent months, senior U.S. officials, including White House Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism Rudolph Atallah and Assistant Secretary of State for West Africa William B. Stevens, visited Bamako to propose American solutions for counterterrorism and private investment initiatives in the Sahel. The Morila deal may therefore reflect Mali’s willingness to engage U.S. investors alongside its existing collaboration with Russia, balancing strategic partnerships while addressing domestic economic and security challenges.

The restart of Morila represents both a symbolic and practical milestone, signaling the government’s commitment to restoring state influence over strategic resources and attracting international investment to bolster economic resilience.

BAMAKO, Mali - Classes resumed across Mali on October 1, but strikes by teachers in several regions have disrupted the school year. The protest stems from unpaid September salaries, with affected employees reportedly listed as “fictitious civil servants” following a government audit.

The audit initially flagged more than 35,000 names, but subsequent verification revealed errors, with many legitimate civil servants mistakenly categorized and denied pay. Despite these measures, union committees in multiple localities have continued their strike until all affected educators receive full payment.

title: Teaching of the French Revolution Suspended in Malian Schools
excerpt: On October 9, 2025, Mali’s Ministry of Education issued an official directive to all directors of the Centre d’Animation, instructing them to suspend the teaching of the French Revolution of 1789 in 9th-grade history classes.
title_en: Teaching of the French Revolution Suspended in Malian Schools
excerpt_en: On October 9, 2025, Mali’s Ministry of Education issued an official directive to all directors of the Centre d’Animation, instructing them to suspend the teaching of the French Revolution of 1789 in 9th-grade history classes.
body_en:
On October 9, 2025, Mali’s Ministry of Education issued an official directive to all directors of the Centre d’Animation, instructing them to suspend the teaching of the French Revolution of 1789 in 9th-grade history classes. This lesson, traditionally the first in the 9th-grade history curriculum, has been a cornerstone of civic education in Mali.

The decision comes amid heightened diplomatic tensions between Mali and France, reflecting a broader push by the transitional government to assert cultural sovereignty. Proponents argue that the measure strengthens national identity by prioritizing Malian perspectives in the school curriculum.

However, critics warn that removing this foundational topic could weaken students’ understanding of democratic principles, civic responsibility, and broader global history. The full implications for educational outcomes remain uncertain, and the Ministry has yet to clarify whether alternative content will replace the French Revolution in the syllabus.

Observers note that this move could have ripple effects on history education nationwide, potentially influencing how Malian students understand both their own national heritage and international historical contexts.

title_en: Trial of Former Prime Minister Moussa Mara Continues in Bamako
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - On Monday, September 29, former Prime Minister Moussa Mara, honorary president of the Yelema Party, appeared before the National Cybercrime Center (PNLC) for his ongoing trial.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - On Monday, September 29, former Prime Minister Moussa Mara, honorary president of the Yelema Party, appeared before the National Cybercrime Center (PNLC) for his ongoing trial. The proceedings were conducted under heightened security and remained tense but orderly between the public prosecutor and Mara’s legal team.

Despite assurances of legal representation, Mara’s request for release was denied. The case has been taken under advisement, with judgment scheduled for October 27. The public prosecutor is seeking a 24-month prison sentence, while the defense has requested full acquittal, arguing there is no legal basis for pretrial detention.

Mara was arrested following a tweet in which he criticized the detention of politicians and civil society leaders, asserting that they were prisoners of conscience. He has remained in preventive detention for nearly three months pending trial.

title: Terrorist Attack Near Bamako Leaves Civilians and Soldiers Dead
excerpt: BAMAKO, Mali - The security situation in central Mali deteriorated further this week following a deadly ambush less than 200 kilometers from the capital.
title_en: Terrorist Attack Near Bamako Leaves Civilians and Soldiers Dead
excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - The security situation in central Mali deteriorated further this week following a deadly ambush less than 200 kilometers from the capital.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - The security situation in central Mali deteriorated further this week following a deadly ambush less than 200 kilometers from the capital. On Wednesday, October 1, armed extremist groups attacked public transport vehicles on the Bamako-Ségou highway that were under military escort.

According to local sources, all members of the escort were killed in the assault, along with several civilians. Among the victims were the wife and two children of the president of the Mopti Administrative Court, who died at the scene. The court’s judge, also among the passengers, sustained gunshot wounds but is reported to be in stable condition.

In total, at least six civilians were confirmed dead, though the Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) have not released an official casualty count for their personnel. The assailants later published images online displaying weapons allegedly seized during the attack - a move consistent with their propaganda tactics aimed at demonstrating battlefield dominance.

The incident underscores the persistent threat posed by militant groups operating across central Mali, even within proximity of Bamako, and highlights the ongoing challenge of securing major transportation routes linking the capital to regional centers.

title: Wave of Explosive Attacks Targets Malian Armed Forces
excerpt: SÉGOU / KIDAL, Mali - Armed extremist groups have intensified their campaign against Malian defense and security forces, employing improvised explosive devices (IEDs) to deadly effect across multiple regions.
title_en: Wave of Explosive Attacks Targets Malian Armed Forces
excerpt_en: SÉGOU / KIDAL, Mali - Armed extremist groups have intensified their campaign against Malian defense and security forces, employing improvised explosive devices (IEDs) to deadly effect across multiple regions.
body_en:
SÉGOU / KIDAL, Mali - Armed extremist groups have intensified their campaign against Malian defense and security forces, employing improvised explosive devices (IEDs) to deadly effect across multiple regions.

On October 2, an army vehicle struck a roadside bomb between Bla and San in the Ségou region, killing all soldiers on board. The following day, a second explosion occurred on the Aguelhoc-Alkit road in the Kidal region, where another Malian Armed Forces (FAMa) vehicle hit a mine. According to militant sources, all nine occupants were killed.

The Malian army has not publicly commented on either incident. However, security analysts note that the back-to-back attacks illustrate the insurgents’ continued ability to disrupt military operations despite recent government offensives.

In response, the army’s general staff reportedly intensified counterterrorism operations across central and northern Mali. While officials acknowledged sustaining significant losses, they emphasized ongoing efforts to maintain pressure on armed religious groups and restore state control in contested zones.

The incident marks a continued escalation in the use of unmanned aerial attacks by armed groups in northern Mali, underscoring the evolving nature of the conflict and the growing importance of air defense capabilities in the country’s counterterrorism strategy.

title: Timbuktu Military Base Welcomes 300 New Recruits
excerpt: TIMBUKTU, Mali - On September 30, the Timbuktu military base officially integrated 300 newly trained soldiers - including 10 women - into the Malian Defense and Security Forces.
title_en: Timbuktu Military Base Welcomes 300 New Recruits
excerpt_en: TIMBUKTU, Mali - On September 30, the Timbuktu military base officially integrated 300 newly trained soldiers - including 10 women - into the Malian Defense and Security Forces.
body_en:
TIMBUKTU, Mali - On September 30, the Timbuktu military base officially integrated 300 newly trained soldiers - including 10 women - into the Malian Defense and Security Forces. The recruits took their oath of allegiance under the national flag during a ceremony held at Camp Fort Cheick Sidi Bekaye, attended by the representative of the Governor of Timbuktu and the regional military commander.

The new soldiers successfully completed a six-month comprehensive training program - the first of its kind in the region - covering weapons handling, tactical maneuvers, and civic education. During the ceremony, the recruits showcased their skills in assembling and disassembling weapons, performed educational skits on drug prevention, and demonstrated combat techniques.

To recognize outstanding performance, the top three trainees received awards for excellence and bravery. The deployment marks a significant reinforcement of security personnel in northern Mali, amid ongoing efforts to stabilize the region and strengthen state authority.

excerpt: MÉNAKA, Mali - In a significant counterterrorism operation, the Malian army, in coordination with security partners from Burkina Faso and Niger, successfully carried out targeted air strikes in the Inarabane area…
title_en: Malian Forces Neutralize Key Daesh Leader Boubacar Demougui in Joint Air Operation
excerpt_en: MÉNAKA, Mali - In a significant counterterrorism operation, the Malian army, in coordination with security partners from Burkina Faso and Niger, successfully carried out targeted air strikes in the Inarabane area…
body_en:
MÉNAKA, Mali - In a significant counterterrorism operation, the Malian army, in coordination with security partners from Burkina Faso and Niger, successfully carried out targeted air strikes in the Inarabane area, southwest of Ménaka. Drones were deployed to precision-target several senior leaders of the Daesh organization, resulting in the elimination of key operatives, including Boubacar Demougui, a high-ranking Daesh commander responsible for northern Ménaka.

Security sources describe Demougui as the operational head of multiple active cells in the region, overseeing logistics, tactical deployments, and management of terrorist detachments. He was reportedly directly involved in the execution of Sidi Barka, president of the Ménaka civil society, an act that sent shockwaves through local communities. Intelligence further confirms that members of Demougui’s family were implicated in the kidnapping of a Spanish hostage in Algeria, highlighting the cross-border scope of his network.

Officials note that the death of Demougui represents a significant blow to Daesh, which maintains influence across northern Mali and the tri-border area encompassing parts of Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso. However, experts caution that the group’s entrenched presence and decentralized structure may allow for rapid leadership replacement, potentially sustaining operational continuity in the region.

The operation underscores the importance of multinational collaboration in counterterrorism efforts and signals a continued commitment by Sahelian states to degrade extremist networks threatening regional stability.

excerpt_en: BAMAKO, Mali - A Moroccan military delegation visited Mali on Tuesday, October 7, 2025, as part of ongoing efforts to enhance defense collaboration between the Kingdom of Morocco and the Republic of Mali.
body_en:
BAMAKO, Mali - A Moroccan military delegation visited Mali on Tuesday, October 7, 2025, as part of ongoing efforts to enhance defense collaboration between the Kingdom of Morocco and the Republic of Mali. The delegation was received at the Directorate of Army Communications, Telecommunications, and Information Technology (DTTIA), where officials discussed the implementation of an electronic border security system, a priority for both nations.

Malian military authorities emphasized the strategic importance of advanced communications and technology for coordinating operations on the ground and ensuring the safety of civilians and property. During the discussions, the Malian side presented the missions, technical capacities, and future ambitions of the DTTIA.

Moroccan intelligence has historically played a role in negotiations for the release of hostages in Mali. Analysts suggest that this new partnership, centered on cutting-edge electronic security systems, will bolster Mali’s counterterrorism capabilities and improve operational efficiency along its borders.

BAMAKO, Mali - On October 8, 2025, eleven officers, including two generals, were formally removed from Mali’s armed and security forces. The decision, signed by transitional President Assimi Goïta, follows the findings of a Council of Inquiry investigating suspicions of a coup d’état.

All eleven officers have been in custody since mid-August for allegedly attempting to destabilize the institutions of the republic. Conclusion: Mali at a Crossroads Between Strategic Resilience and the Threat of Collapse

The period from September 29 to October 11, 2025, reveals a Mali facing a multidimensional crisis, where growing insecurity is catalyzing profound economic and social destabilization. The country is navigating between determined efforts to assert its sovereignty and a reality on the ground that threatens the very foundations of the state.

On the security front, the situation has deteriorated considerably. Extremist groups are intensifying their attacks, employing various tactics (ambushes, explosive devices, drones) and extending their influence to the gates of Bamako. The assassinations of prominent figures and kidnappings demonstrate the audacity of the attackers, while the Malian armed forces, despite targeted successes such as the neutralization of terrorist leaders, are suffering significant losses.

This insecurity has devastating economic consequences, materialized by a terrorist blockade on hydrocarbons. The country is plunged into a severe fuel and electricity crisis, paralyzing transportation, the economy, and essential services, raising fears of a shutdown. At the same time, the government is striving to lay the foundations for long-term economic resilience, as evidenced by the strategic revival of the Morila gold mine with an American partner and regional integration efforts within the ESA.

Politically, the transitional government is pursuing a dual strategy: consolidating its authority internally, marked by the dissolution of political parties and firmness in the face of any opposition, and building a new regional security architecture with its ESA partners. On the international stage, Bamako is navigating diplomatic tensions, particularly with France, and pragmatic diversification of its partnerships (United States, Morocco, Mauritania).

Finally, the human cost of this instability is immense. The education system is in ruins, with more than half a million children out of school and teachers on strike. The daily lives of the population are directly affected by shortages and rising costs.

In summary, this report paints a picture of a state in the midst of a struggle for its sovereignty and survival, engaged on several fronts: military, economic, and diplomatic. While strategic initiatives are being launched, security pressures and their immediate repercussions on the population and the economy pose an existential threat to Mali's short-term stability.

excerpt_en: Bamako, Mali-President Abdourahamane Tiani’s visit to Mali marked a critical juncture in institutionalizing the AES, a new regional security and development bloc designed to address cross-border instability in the Sahel.
body_en:
Bamako, Mali-President Abdourahamane Tiani’s visit to Mali marked a critical juncture in institutionalizing the AES, a new regional security and development bloc designed to address cross-border instability in the Sahel. His arrival at Modibo Keïta-Sénou International Airport was met with full military honors by Malian President General Assimi Goïta, signaling the strategic priority both nations attach to this alliance.

The closed-door discussions focused on three pillars of cooperation:

Integrated Security Architecture - planning intelligence-sharing protocols, standardizing military equipment, and establishing a unified command for cross-border counterinsurgency operations

Economic Sovereignty - finalizing technical frameworks for the AES Investment and Development Bank, including headquarters, operational structures, and governance oversight.

Diplomatic Alignment - harmonizing positions on regional organizations and international forums to consolidate the AES as a coherent political and security actor.

“All preliminary steps are clear - headquarters, structures, and mechanisms. Everything will be finalized, God willing, at our next meeting.”

Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso -The visit continued with a stop in Burkina Faso to meet Captain Ibrahim Traoré, reinforcing the AES’s tripartite dimension. Discussions emphasized governance, development cooperation, and regional security, signaling that AES ambitions extend beyond military coordination to a holistic Sahelian governance model rooted in sovereignty, stability, and development.

body_en:
NIAMEY - Niger’s ongoing political transition continues to shape the country’s governance landscape, as the administration balances military authority with growing public demands for democratic restoration and economic relief.

Since the 2023 transition, the government has relied on the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland (CNSP), the ruling military body central to state administration. Its visible role in official ceremonies and the appointment of military figures to key ministerial positions underscore the leadership’s focus on maintaining institutional control during this critical period.

While this approach has preserved stability and continuity, it underscores a delicate tension between prioritizing security and addressing citizens’ calls for political inclusion and socio-economic improvement. The coming months will test the transitional government’s ability to sustain order while laying the groundwork for a more accountable and participatory political system.

title: President Tiani’s Visit to Téra Highlights Strategic Push for Regional Stability and Development
excerpt: TÉRA, Niger - On October 5, 2025, President Abdourahamane Tiani visited Téra Department in a move that extended beyond routine provincial oversight.
title_en: President Tiani’s Visit to Téra Highlights Strategic Push for Regional Stability and Development
excerpt_en: TÉRA, Niger - On October 5, 2025, President Abdourahamane Tiani visited Téra Department in a move that extended beyond routine provincial oversight.
body_en:
TÉRA, Niger - On October 5, 2025, President Abdourahamane Tiani visited Téra Department in a move that extended beyond routine provincial oversight. The visit underscored the government’s strategic intent to reassert state presence, revitalize infrastructure, and strengthen security coordination in a region critical to national cohesion and cross-border stability.

During the visit, President Tiani highlighted the severe degradation of the 187-kilometer Téra-Niamey road, calling it a major development bottleneck. The route, essential for trade, health access, and education, has suffered years of neglect, directly affecting livelihoods across the department. He also addressed Téra’s chronic water supply crisis, where the local treatment facility operates at just 45% capacity due to maintenance deficits and power shortages, leaving nearly 85,000 residents without reliable access to clean water. The president pledged “case-by-case solutions,” signaling a pragmatic, localized approach, though analysts caution that systemic reform may be required for lasting impact.

On security, Tiani engaged with officers of Defense Zone No. 9, which continues to confront asymmetric threats from militant groups along the western border. Official reports indicate 23 security incidents in the past quarter - a 17% decline from the previous period - yet Téra remains Niger’s second most-affected region.

The visit reflected a broader strategy of field-based governance, combining infrastructure rehabilitation, security engagement, and symbolic state presence to consolidate authority and address persistent regional disparities.

Political Messaging: A Shift Toward Direct, Hands-On Governance

President Tiani’s trip also revealed an evolution in the administration’s communication style. By engaging directly with local populations through unscripted interactions, the president bypassed traditional media channels, delivering unfiltered narratives and emphasizing immediate, tangible solutions.

The approach reinforced personal accountability, framing regional challenges as requiring his direct intervention. This hands-on communication strategy strengthens Tiani’s image as an active, approachable leader while centralizing responsibility and authority within the presidential office, signaling a governance model that prioritizes visibility, responsiveness, and concentrated decision-making.

excerpt: NIAMEY - On October 7, 2025, municipal authorities in Niamey unveiled a comprehensive reform targeting informal commercial activities, signaling a major step toward modernizing urban governance under Niger’s…
title_en: Niamey Launches Ambitious Urban Governance Reforms
excerpt_en: NIAMEY - On October 7, 2025, municipal authorities in Niamey unveiled a comprehensive reform targeting informal commercial activities, signaling a major step toward modernizing urban governance under Niger’s…
body_en:
NIAMEY - On October 7, 2025, municipal authorities in Niamey unveiled a comprehensive reform targeting informal commercial activities, signaling a major step toward modernizing urban governance under Niger’s transitional government.

Led by the Delegate Administrator, the initiative aims to formalize approximately 3,500 informal traders, integrating them into regulated markets. The policy is expected to increase municipal revenues through licensing while improving labor conditions for traders.

Beyond economic formalization, the reform addresses public space congestion in key markets such as Katako, Grand Marché, and Pays-Bas, where unregulated trading has historically restricted emergency access by up to 40%.

The program also incorporates social protection measures, including designated trading zones in each district equipped with basic sanitation facilities. This hybrid approach, combining regulation with service delivery, reflects a shift toward inclusive and pragmatic urban management in Niger’s capital.

title: Germany Strengthens Local Governance and Peacebuilding Efforts in Niger
excerpt: Niger and Germany reaffirmed their strategic partnership this week as Minister of State Toumba met with a delegation from the German Development Bank (KfW) to review ongoing cooperation projects.
title_en: Germany Strengthens Local Governance and Peacebuilding Efforts in Niger
excerpt_en: Niger and Germany reaffirmed their strategic partnership this week as Minister of State Toumba met with a delegation from the German Development Bank (KfW) to review ongoing cooperation projects.
body_en:
Niger and Germany reaffirmed their strategic partnership this week as Minister of State Toumba met with a delegation from the German Development Bank (KfW) to review ongoing cooperation projects. The meeting underscored the continuity of European engagement in Niger, emphasizing local governance, conflict sensitivity, and sustainable investment.

Germany’s development support currently targets 35 municipal governments across six regions, focusing on local revenue generation, participatory planning, and public service monitoring. This reflects Berlin’s growing commitment to strengthening sub-national institutions as engines of stability and accountability.

A notable feature of this cooperation is its conflict-sensitive approach, prioritizing peace and social cohesion-a response to earlier aid models that had unintentionally fueled local tensions through uneven resource distribution.

With an active KfW portfolio exceeding €125 million, Germany remains a key partner in sectors such as renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, and municipal infrastructure. These investments align with Niger’s national development goals, while maintaining operational independence from the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) framework, ensuring flexibility in implementation.

This engagement highlights Europe’s evolving role in Niger’s transition, moving beyond humanitarian assistance toward institutional resilience and sustainable growth.

excerpt: Niger is deepening its multilateral partnerships, as reflected in recent engagements with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and UN Women.
title_en: Niger Strengthens Multilateral Ties with UN Agencies
excerpt_en: Niger is deepening its multilateral partnerships, as reflected in recent engagements with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and UN Women.
body_en:
Niger is deepening its multilateral partnerships, as reflected in recent engagements with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and UN Women.

In the health sector, discussions with UNFPA spotlighted Niger’s pioneering policy declaring maternal and perinatal mortality a public health emergency. Analysts report that this initiative has mobilized $2.7 million in domestic funds via a national telethon, alongside an additional $3.2 million reallocated from ministerial budgets.

Meanwhile, talks with UN Women focused on implementing Niger’s National Gender Policy within the broader context of the country’s “refoundation” agenda. Key initiatives under this framework include programs promoting women’s economic empowerment in agribusiness value chains and gender-responsive budgeting across 12 pilot municipalities.

Both UN agencies stressed the importance of aligning their efforts with Niger’s current transition roadmap, rather than adhering strictly to previous UN Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) commitments. Observers say this reflects a pragmatic approach by the UN to adapt to the nation’s evolving political landscape.

title: Government Faces Constraints in Responding to Socio-Economic Challenges

title_en: Government Faces Constraints in Responding to Socio-Economic Challenges
excerpt_en: Niger’s administration is struggling to address mounting socio-economic pressures, limited by structural and fiscal constraints.
body_en:
Niger’s administration is struggling to address mounting socio-economic pressures, limited by structural and fiscal constraints.

Reforms to petroleum subsidies have increased household financial burdens while offering limited budgetary flexibility, particularly as uranium revenues decline. Meanwhile, the national social safety net program reaches only 12% of the country’s extremely poor households, leaving vast segments of the population vulnerable.

The lack of institutionalized tripartite social dialogue since the recent political transition has further hampered structured engagement between the government, employers, and workers, complicating efforts to manage labor relations effectively.

title_en: Niger Advances Energy Sector Transformation with AfDB Partnership
excerpt_en: Niger has signed a $144.7 million (CFAF 80.9 billion) agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB) aimed at enhancing energy sector governance, competitiveness, and access.
body_en:
Niger has signed a $144.7 million (CFAF 80.9 billion) agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB) aimed at enhancing energy sector governance, competitiveness, and access.

Under the agreement, Niger aims to raise national electricity access from 22.5% to 30% by 2026 and develop 240 MW of solar energy capacity by 2030. The initiative also focuses on governance reforms to improve transparency and revenue mobilization, while strengthening private sector competitiveness through a more stable and reliable energy supply.

AfDB’s investment adopts a holistic approach to Niger’s chronic energy deficit, encompassing rural and urban grid expansion, solar infrastructure development, and modernized transmission networks. The program also targets governance improvements within the Société Nigérienne d'Électricité (NIGELEC), enhancing procurement transparency and updating regulatory frameworks. Economically, the partnership is expected to lower production costs, ensure reliable energy supply, and create new jobs in the renewable energy sector.
